In the foregoing—the closing section of Chapter Three—it was mentioned that: for the "Hanoi work," large quantities of arms and ammunition had already been brought in, in batches, by trusted men dispatched severally along the sea and air routes; and that we had received a telegraphed instruction from Mr. Dai Yunong: "Make such preparations as are necessary; but on no account act rashly"—and so forth. That is to say, although the weapons had been brought in, they were only to be held in readiness and not used, unless there should be some further instruction.

We were, of course, scrupulous in obeying orders; how should we have dared to run wild? Under these circumstances, the most important thing was still the reconnaissance and disposition before action: we needed to get a clear picture of Wang's daily life and habits; and then there was the assignment and employment of personnel, in the hope that every comrade at the work might give of his particular strengths. The business of reconnaissance and re-survey was still entrusted to Tang Yingjie, who had a special skill in it, and I gave him plain instructions that, however arduous or perilous it might be, he must contrive to get inside Wang's residence and look about; and if that proved truly impossible, then at the very least he must vault onto the rooftop and, hanging head-down in the "rolled-up-blind" posture, spy in that way. As for the allotment of manpower, two more comrades had lately been transferred in from Kunming, both action men; one of them, a Comrade Zhang, was a native of Meixian in Guangdong—as I recall, I still remember his broad face, his large eyes, a distinctly prosperous look about him; the other comrade I cannot call back even the least image of, and I offer this comrade my apologies, though I still mean to make inquiries. Because our own quarters already held seven men and truly could hold no more, we lodged these two elsewhere, listed them as reserves, and had Luqiao keep in touch with them.
At this point the "Hanoi work" entered upon a new phase. We were now in a "state of combat readiness," quietly awaiting the word of command.

Here the writer must make one thing plain: this "combat readiness" was no more than a precautionary measure taken by Mr. Dai on behalf of the Juntong; it did not signify that the central authorities had already reached a final decision to sanction Wang Jingwei. As for what part Mr. Dai played in this historic action, the writer does not presume to conjecture out of thin air. Better to write of the things I myself understood, and so fulfill my original purpose.

There is one passage of events that I had not, at first, meant to write out; in the several decades gone by, the "Hanoi story" has been told too many times, yet this particular thing was never once brought up.

But since the point now is to furnish historical material, then one ought to tell it plainly and truthfully; for if I do not tell it, I not only conceal a fact, but this passage of events will also be buried forever and pass out of all knowledge.
As to whether the telling of it may have some ill effect—since standpoint, angle, and view differ, each will surely have his own say, the benevolent seeing benevolence and the wise seeing wisdom.

Besides, this too was a part of our "Hanoi work"; since the thing did happen, it is of no little interest in the telling, and it can moreover reflect the level of our science and technology in those days, together with certain none-too-clever methods of ours.

From the time we received Mr. Dai's telegram bidding us make ready for action, Brother Yu Lexing was itching to try his hand; he urged strongly that a "soft action" be used to accomplish our end. Now, the means adopted in carrying out sanction work fall broadly into two great classes: the first is the "loud weapon," meaning to strike with firearms; the second is the "silent weapon," meaning to kill with knife and axe, or to poison with a toxin. Which is used depends on the defensive situation of the sanction target and on the circumstances of the moment. What Mr. Yu now advocated was the latter, which for convenience I here call the "soft action." In my own heart I was much against it, yet I could not openly show my opposition either—another of those things hard to deal with. In the Shi Yousan sanction case in "Rooting Out Traitors in the North," the Tianjin Station and the Beiping Station had both suffered a bitter lesson on just this account, several comrades sacrificed one after another, and the outcome in every case a failure; and then, as for my own temper, I truly did not care to take up so nearly underhanded a means, always feeling it wanted the openness and honor of a straight, hard fight. Even when the end is gained by sniping, that is no different from "a punishment justly and openly carried out"; whereas if one uses so underhanded a means, then even should it succeed by luck, the outside world is bound to buzz with conjecture, and what would people make of us then? The more so since its reliability, being impossible to command, was open to doubt.

In fact, my opposition may be said to have been superfluous. I ought to have thought long before of this: that Mr. Dai's very reason for sending a doctor of chemistry was that this stratagem was already in his bag of tricks; and Brother Yu Lexing, too, said again and again that this was the greatest charge Mr. Dai had committed to him. Just so—and it was not only that our superiors so intended: of late, even the chemicals to be used had been shipped in. Was it not already mentioned in the foregoing, in that line, "large quantities of firearms and ammunition brought in by the various routes"? Perhaps the writer did not make it plain: the "firearms and ammunition" spoken of there were not just two things, but in fact four or five kinds: for firearms, handguns; for edged tools, hatchets, sharp blades, and steel saws; for shells, cartridges; and for medicine, a deadly poison.

Before setting about it, Brother Yu Lexing and I exchanged views in detail on one occasion. The first thing we had to consider was whether there was any such opportunity at all, and whether we could contrive to make one. On this point neither of us could for the moment put forward any concrete plan, so we had no choice but to consult that mysterious personage, Mr. Xu, and see what he thought before going further. To our surprise he too warmly approved of the method, and his reasons were very simple: he held that, whatever the result, success or failure, such a course could at most give rise to a little conjecture, and would never stir up too much trouble. At the same time he volunteered, offering to find us a suitable opportunity.

To gather wisdom from many, I spoke of the matter separately with Brother Cen Jiazhuo, on the question of what would decide success or failure. He kept silence for a long while and would give no opinion either way, which was strange indeed. Then at last he said: "I am afraid it will be labor spent for nothing; for unless we can get someone inside Wang's household to answer to us, it will be very hard to bring off well; and yet to find a collaborator among Wang's kin and servants is very nearly an impossible thing. What do you think?" Our views were close. And yet a man keen on such a course will not give up his heart's desire till he reaches the Yellow River!

That night, before turning in, as I chatted with Luqiao, I brought the matter up too—this was not an exchange of views, but had somewhat the flavor of one friend unburdening his heart to another. He agreed with me, of course; and being a hearty, open man, he held that if a thing was to be done, it should be done with a will and to the full.
Apart from the few persons named above, none of the other comrades knew of this matter, nor was there any need to tell them.

To take up the thread again: Brother Lexing was skilled only in the knowledge of drugs; as to how the drug was to be got into the body of the target—which required the separate contriving of a delivery channel before it could take effect—in that he could only stand in an advisory place and offer a suggestion or two. In practice it still depended on Mr. Xu's side to push things forward. To speed the business along, and also to steady my confidence, Brother Lexing spared no pains in explaining the drug he had successfully developed; he said gravely: "It has been tested many times over, and both its potency and its effect are excellent; so long as it can be got into the other party, I can guarantee there will be no slip."

So saying, Brother Lexing took out a paper case, and on opening it there were, inside, three glass bottles ranged neatly—three bottles alike, all of a colorless liquid. Only, the bottles were labeled, each differently, A, B, and C. Brother Lexing carefully drew the stopper from bottle A, gave it a shake, and explained: "This bottle holds the principal drug; the other two are ingredients. In using it, one must, according to the difference of the object and the situation, freely adjust the dose, heavier or lighter. This liquid is colorless and odorless, and has a sediment too; you must not bring it near the nose to smell, for that also would poison you. If this stuff is injected into the body, a single drop can kill at once; mixed into food and swallowed, it will very quickly bring numbness of the nerves and loss of consciousness, and unless aid is given at once, the man will never wake again." Having finished, he very carefully put it away and set it back in its place. Then he added: "Exposure to light or to heat is sure to weaken the drug's effect."

He talked for a long while, and I could only lend a respectful ear. For I was neither equipped for a scholarly discussion, nor was it convenient to betray even the least particle of doubt; Brother Lexing was a man with whom one could not jest, and his self-regard was especially strong, so that a single ill-fitting word would bring on his displeasure. At this moment I was reckoning in my heart: Brother Lexing was in deep earnest, and I must on no account fob him off; whether the thing would do or not, I must take up further with Mr. Xu, in the hope of reaching a satisfactory conclusion.

I went alone to meet Mr. Xu, and he said he had just been about to look for me. Mr. Xu told me, unable to wait: "There is a bread-delivery man; I wonder whether use might be made of him." I asked Mr. Xu to go on in detail.

"This bread man is a local. Every morning he delivers bread to the bakery's subscribers. Any household may subscribe; if we wished to subscribe, so long as it were within the city, we could of course have him deliver daily as well. And if we needed two deliveries a day, I think he would be all the more glad of it.

"That in itself is nothing; what is worth noting is that the Wang residence has taken out a subscription too. This you can look into and verify; it will not be untrue. If there is no difficulty, might one not put one's wits to work? I think it should serve.
"If you have a mind to try it, you have only to talk with Mr. Zeng and you can find this bread man, for his own house has subscribed too, and has done so for a long while." So said Mr. Xu.
I thanked him, and promised that after I had gone into it with Mr. Yu I would go and make contact with Mr. Zeng.

I passed Mr. Xu's words on to Brother Lexing; he thought a moment and asked me to work with him and first make a trial. Before setting about the trial, I could not but put forward several questions to which I had to have definite answers:
First: since we ourselves cannot bake bread, how are we to get a liquid substance mixed into the bread?
This was the one and only reason we absolutely had to make a trial.
Second: how are we to get the drugged bread, by way of that bread-delivery man, to the Wang household?
Brother Lexing's notion was that a "swap" would be best; and if the swap could not be managed, then the delivery man could be bought over.

I held this needed weighing, for there was no full assurance of getting the drugged bread to the Wang house; and if by mischance it were delivered to the wrong household, we should not only harm the innocent but ruin the affair as well—that would be dreadful. As for buying him over, the hope was slight, and afterward there would surely be a thread to trace; as the saying goes, "the monk may run, but the temple cannot"—so we must make ready beforehand.

Third: even if the drugged bread were delivered to the Wang house just as usual, how could we be sure that Wang alone would eat it? Should the husband and wife both dine together, to do away with one Chen Bijun besides would be no great matter; but if the whole family, kin and servants included, should share it—would that not drag in the innocent?
On this point Brother Lexing, by the look of him, was much of the mind that one could not see to everything; yet he could not bring himself to say so.

These questions, study them how we might, could get no answer; and since they could get no answer, what sort of plan was that? It could hardly stand at all. Yet Brother Lexing still held that there was no harm in first getting a loaf and trying.

Fourth: it had of course occurred to us—why not start from the baker himself? On this too we made many suppositions, back and forth, and none would do; unless one concocted it oneself, one must on no account leave it in another's hands.
To tell the truth, I was never very keen on this method; but since in fact I could not prevail against Brother Lexing, I could only give it a try for the once.

For the matter of ordering the bread, I went, as Mr. Xu had said, to find Mr. Zeng, and he said: "Mr. Xu has already given word. This bakery is close by; it is best to go straight to them to order, and tell them to deliver at the set time to a place appointed—that will do." Mr. Zeng was right; in this way one would avoid entanglements later.

The ordering of the bread I entrusted to Wei Chunfeng, and he brought back a good many kinds, big and small: there was the oblong pillow loaf, the small Russian dinner roll, some pointed at both ends and some plaited like fried-dough twists. I did not grow up eating bread, and which sort might serve for breakfast I did not know; according to Lexing and Chunfeng, it was mostly the square kind, though it went by each man's liking too. Let that pass for now; we would settle it after the trial—it would be easy enough, in any case, to make sure which kind the Wang house had ordered.

The trial was conducted by Brother Lexing, with me assisting from the side; we did not let Wei Chunfeng take part—in things of this kind, the fewer who know, the better. Our trial was not so solemn as one might imagine, yet it was no joke either; somewhere between the two. The two of us shut ourselves in the bathroom to carry it out. First Brother Lexing took out a bottle of the drug and set it on the little tea-table; then he brought a syringe and set the square loaf whole upon the table, while I crouched on the floor and steadied the loaf with both hands to keep it from shifting. He drew about half a cc of the liquid from the small bottle and, very carefully and slowly, injected it into the loaf, then withdrew the needle and injected at another spot. After that he shook his head, as if to say: it won't do!
Brother Lexing carried the loaf off to the sitting room, saying: "In a while we'll cut it open and see whether there's any change."

Out of curiosity I asked Brother Lexing: "Shall I try that loaf pointed at both ends myself?" He said: "Do be careful—on no account let it splash on you, in case of accident." So I too used the syringe he had just used, and drew a little of the liquid from the small bottle; holding it up to look, I saw it was half again less than what he had drawn. Just as I was about to inject it into the loaf, my hand—not being as practiced as his, and perhaps because this loaf was baked a little too long, its crust too hard; or else because the needle slipped aside off it—this thrust drove not the liquid in, but sent it spraying back. Whether it truly splashed onto my face, or was some trick of a frightened mind, I do not know; but it gave me a dreadful fright. I threw down the syringe at once, hastily turned on the tap, bent over, shut my eyes, and gave myself a fierce dousing under the shower-head; then secretly bit my tongue with my teeth, and finding I still felt the pain, at last set my mind at ease. Looking round, I saw Brother Lexing already standing in the bathroom doorway, watching my every move; but he could not well say anything, and pretended nothing of the sort had just happened. Still, I went on muttering to myself: might it not, after all, come on in a while?

Brother Lexing called me into the sitting room to inspect the loaf that had just been injected. First he broke off a small piece by hand and examined it closely under a magnifying glass; no change could be seen. Then he took the bread-knife and cut two or three slices, and going over them slice by slice, at the third slice something was wrong: with the naked eye one could see pale-yellow spots in the crumb, and at the part where the injected liquid had gone in it had even set into lumps the size of soybeans; without so much as touching it, one knew it had nearly hardened. Brother Lexing cut a few more slices from the other end of the loaf, and they were much the same as the end already seen. At this he showed a look of disappointment, and shook his head at me without ceasing, meaning: it won't do—how could anyone eat a loaf like this with an easy mind! It fails at the very first pass, and all the schemes to follow may as well be scrapped.

Brother Lexing was still unwilling to give up; he wanted to try once more. By his reckoning, if the injected dose were reduced and the injection sites evenly increased, one might correspondingly avoid the phenomenon just seen. For Brother Lexing's working spirit I had, of course, all respect; but as for the drug-based "soft action," my interest had long since flagged, and I could truly raise no enthusiasm for it. Only consider: even were we to try again by his design, not only was there no possibility of so long a stretch of time for the arrangements, but a loaf stuck with several dozen needle-marks—what sort of thing would that become? Was one really to suppose the household would see nothing of it?
After a round of deliberation, the two of us at last agreed together that it would not do, and gave it up.

Next Brother Lexing put forward yet another method; he asked whether I had time, so that he might give a demonstration of a second approach. I could not say I did not wish to hear it, yet in my heart I was truly a little impatient.

From a wrapped little box he took out a metal object, one I had never seen before. It was not large in bulk, cylindrical in form; held in the palm, it showed only a little; a man with a large hand could grasp it whole in his fist, so that with neither end showing it became a big fist. On top there was a cap; unscrewed, there was another tightly fastened cover beneath; lift that off, and at the top were many small holes, much like the little bottle for sprinkling pepper—though not to be used as one sprinkles pepper into soup. Brother Lexing toyed with the little bottle in his hand and explained to me at the same time, saying: "This too is a liquid, of very great volatility; with heat, its volatility is the greater; drawn into the body, it can bring on death through shock. If it is set in the bathroom, and moreover a hot bath is being taken, the evaporation is especially quick, and then the effect is surer still."

Before Brother Lexing could go on, I had already guessed his design through and through: he meant to set this thing in the Wang household's bathroom, and once Wang had taken a hot bath, he would never come out of it again. Brother Lexing, too, read something of this in my look, and forestalling me, he broke open the very difficulty I doubted, saying: "Of course it is not so simple. How to get this thing into their bathroom should be the first problem to solve; and on this point I have a plan of my own. Only give your consent, and I will first go and feel out the ground; then, according to the result, we can decide."

This matter went no further at the time, and there was then no sequel to it. More than two years later, by November of the thirtieth year, when Chen Bijun had me brought up for interrogation at Shanghai, she put it to me: "You put a little canister in my bathroom—what was that for?" Her asking this left me quite dumbfounded.
This is a "later matter"; just what it was all about I plan to write of in detail in "Nameless Heroes, Book Three."
In the small hours of the nineteenth of March of the twenty-eighth year, at about two o'clock, was a crucial and important moment.

Mr. Dai Yunong had telegraphed from Chongqing, and it was Brother Fang Bingxi who, in the dead of night, brought it in person to my quarters. Though the telegram was marked with the secrecy grade "decipher personally," since the cipher-book was kept at Brother Bingxi's and I had long since authorized him to decipher on my behalf, what he handed me was only a little slip of paper in plain text.
Do not make light of this little slip: in the terms of our work it carried the weight of a thousand jun—this was the "sanction order," as yet unstamped with any seal!

The original wording of the "sanction order" I can no longer clearly recall; the gist was: "Proceed at once to visit severe sanction upon the traitor Wang Jingwei." In just these dozen-odd words were contained three main elements: "proceed at once" marked the time, that is, "from this moment"; "upon the traitor Wang" indicated the "work target"; "visit severe sanction" meant "to inflict the heaviest penalty—death." This was the first time Mr. Dai had used the word "traitor" in his designation of Wang Jingwei, and in that sense he had fixed upon him the guilt of "rebellion." And with this the "Hanoi work" too entered its final phase.

The comrades we had been transferred to Hanoi were, in the nature of their work, weighted from the first toward "hard action"; and from this one may see that Mr. Dai, in his disposition of personnel, must have had a purpose long in mind. Yet he was but one working department—or say, one unit within the special-service work—and over a matter so grave and so pressing he had, of course, no final power of decision. As for how the whole process went, the writer, a mere field hand, knew all the less; at the most he grasped, from what he actually experienced, but a small part. The foregoing made it very clear: at the outset the task was confined to watching Wang's movements and reconnoitering his activities, and this stretch of time ran nearly forty or fifty days; it was not until early March that we received Mr. Dai's instruction bidding us prepare to sanction Wang, with the strict charge that, before the "sanction order" came, we were not to act rashly. Tracing the past back along this course, one can very plainly see: at first the hope had been that Wang might rein in at the cliff's edge, change his first purpose, heed the counsel given, and set out for Europe; this, like the several tiffs of former days, might—when the thing had blown over—still leave room in future for joint counsel on affairs of state. That was why the central authorities sent men to Hanoi more than once, bearing passport, travel funds, and the like, hoping Wang would soon set forth; and the record shows that Wang, though he seized the pretext to pour out his grievances to the envoys and gave no firm answer, yet did leave behind (not accept) the passport and funds—that is, he did not flatly refuse. On this point the writer received several telegrams to verify the matter, and paid particular heed to Wang's movements; which just reflects how very seriously the Chongqing side did regard his comings and goings. By now we knew that relations between the Japanese government and Wang were at a low ebb, and that the new Hiranuma cabinet in Japan even made a show of deliberately cold-shouldering Wang; so that Wang grew somewhat irresolute. By our understanding, he did once mean to leave Hanoi, go by way of Saigon, and cross over to France—only to be vetoed by his wife, Chen Bijun. Was it, then, because he would not leave that the resolve to kill was stirred? In fact it was not so simple as that; the several chief reasons in it I will bring forward for a full reckoning once we have brought the "Hanoi work" to a stage's close.

So I drafted a brief reply, to the effect: "Telegram number X received and understood; proceeding actively at once," and handed it straightway to Brother Bingxi, asking him to take it back and send it. At the same time I first called together the six comrades who lodged with us—Wang Luqiao, Yu Jiansheng, Zhang Fengyi, Tang Yingjie, Chen Bangguo, and Chen Buyun—and passed round for reading the telegraphed order just received. When all had seen it, I signed to Luqiao to burn it there and then, and we sat down to take counsel on the great plan of the work. In using the word "counsel" here I speak but modestly; in fact it was I alone who announced my personal decision before them all, and none of the six comrades present voiced any dissent—no, not so much as a word by way of addition.

To speak again of "the sanction order being handed down": in our minds this was, from the first, a thing bound to come sooner or later, no surprise at all, and might well have been dealt with in an easy, unhurried way; and the work itself was, for that matter, not so very hard, the more so as so many men had come, one lot after another. Yet somehow—I cannot tell how—it was as though a formless pressure stifled the heart of every man. Was it that my bearing was too grave? Or was it that this mission was too great? For a while the whole houseful of us had its air turned stiff and cold.
The matters I announced at the time were these:
In obedience to the instruction of our superiors, it is resolved to take hard action, and to visit severe sanction upon the traitor to the nation, Wang Jingwei;
Until some more suitable ground of action be found, Wang's residence shall for the present be the target of attack;
Once we set out, I myself shall direct and command; when the several comrades lose direct contact with me, Comrade Wang Luqiao is designated to command, with Comrade Yu Jiansheng assisting;
After entering Wang's residence, Comrade Tang Yingjie shall guide the two Comrades Wang Luqiao and Yu Jiansheng toward the target, and thereupon join the ranks of the action;
Comrades Zhang Fengyi, Chen Bangguo, and Chen Buyun, three in all, shall severally take up guard and cover, each man's position to be designated by Comrade Wang Luqiao;

Afterward, withdraw as each sees fit, and reassemble at the original starting point. Should any, by mischance, be arrested by the local police, on no account reveal his identity; the other details bearing on this shall be laid down more particularly by the two Comrades Wang Luqiao and Yu Jiansheng, together with the several comrades;
As for the time of setting out—from this moment, let each comrade, in a state of combat readiness, await notice.

Besides this, we had two newly arrived comrades who were not present; in the disposition, since the manpower was already enough to draw upon, they were listed as reserves and for the time being not notified.

When I had done announcing, and asked the comrades once more for their views, only Luqiao spoke a word: "We all do as you say!" For the rest, the others made no sign. By the look of the sky, it was already faintly light.

I bade them each rest, husband their strength, and make what personal preparations they would, but on no account to go off, lest they could not be found when wanted. Then I went to the lodging of the two Brothers Yu Lexing and Cen Jiazhuo, to convey our superiors' instruction and ask the two of them their views.

Brother Jiazhuo, ever deep and reserved, now declared himself quite plainly: "If there is anything you need me to do, pray do not stand on ceremony—only assign me my work." This set me a poser; for the moment I could not think of a fitting word to answer him, since, as regards the setting-out, I had already made my arrangements, and to ask him to command would be hardly seemly, and might breed some misunderstanding. Then of a sudden a thought struck me—there was, in fact, the needful matter of a "second-line disposition"; and in this way Brother Lexing's task, too, fell naturally into place along with it.
So I asked the two Brothers Lexing and Jiazhuo to draw up close, and put my thoughts to them in all sincerity:

First, I gave an account of the "hard action" disposition already decided on, in the hope that it would not be changed again; yet I could not warrant that this plan would surely succeed. Should it miscarry, I might not be able to go on directing in person, and at that time the two Brothers Jiazhuo and Lexing could still marshal the strength in hand and, taking up the task afresh, complete the mission our superiors had committed to us. My design was as follows:
Let the two Brothers Jiazhuo and Lexing take joint charge; if one man must be named to be responsible, let Mr. Dai make the final decision;
Let Comrade Fang Bingxi still take charge of the business-side work, and manage the communications besides;
Through Fang Bingxi's introduction, get in touch with the two Comrades Cao Shi'ang and Tan Tianqian;
The two reserve action men surnamed Zhang, newly arrived at Hanoi and not yet assigned work, to be placed under Brother Jiazhuo's command;
For all reserve funds and the firearms and ammunition and the like, let the two Brothers Jiazhuo and Lexing deal directly with Brother Bingxi;

As for the special personage Mr. Xu, put in touch by Mr. Dai, contact may likewise be kept up through Bingxi's relaying; only, whether Mr. Xu himself consents, there is no harm in first having Bingxi sound him out;
As for the working connections we have employed, Mr. Zeng and Wei Chunfeng and the rest—whether they can still be of use hereafter can, for the present, only be left in reserve;
After this action is over, let all those who withdraw in safety and are not yet exposed apply to the two Brothers Jiazhuo and Lexing, to be reassigned work.

When the two of them had heard out my plan and decision, neither would commit himself either way—no wonder, for what expression would have been just the right one to make? And indeed, however things might develop, our superiors would be sure to give instructions, and no man, whoever he might be, would dare of course to act on his own authority.

Before leaving, I charged the two Brothers Jiazhuo and Lexing that the date of taking action must wait upon an exchange of views with that Mr. Xu before it could be fixed; by my own reckoning, it would be within these two or three days. Let them be prepared in mind.

I went again to seek out Brother Fang Bingxi, and repeated to him, for his reference, the charge I had just given the two Brothers Cen and Yu. Then I asked Brother Bingxi to go with me to meet Mr. Xu. In our "Hanoi work" we leaned on Mr. Xu in too many things; the thing about to happen there was, at bottom, no need to notify him of beforehand, but the aftereffects would fall for the most part on him to bear; so that whether in reason, in duty, or in the seizing of the moment, I felt for my own part that I ought to make it plain to him, and only so be easy in mind.

Mr. Xu did not find it sudden; for from the signs—the men sent from the various routes, the arms shipped in by sea and air—he had long foreseen this move. On it he too gave a view of his own, saying: "If one speaks from the legal standpoint of ridding the country of a scourge, this is of course a mode of sanction one is driven to in a case past all help; but if it touches on political entanglements, it is not the wisest way of solving the thing." Mr. Xu spoke rightly, to be sure; yet I had to add, with heavier stress and in affirmation: "Wang's affair is by no means a mere political question; it touches the nation's law besides. Very plainly, in a state of war between two countries, he has betrayed his own nation and colluded with the enemy to sue for peace!"

In truth this was not the point we had come to discuss; it was only that one word led to another and we restated our standpoint once more. So we turned the talk to the main business. Mr. Xu hoped we would do the thing cleanly and neatly, on no account draggle-tailed, stirring up a mass of trouble hard for him to handle; for the rest, it was all one to him. My own wish was just as Mr. Xu conceived it: to make it, so far as we could, go smoothly and to our mind.

I told Mr. Xu: "Since our superiors have handed down the sanction order, I have roughly decided to take action within these two or three days; whether the timing is suitable I do not know. If Mr. Xu has any counsel to give, pray tell me plainly—all is open to discussion." Mr. Xu said: "There is nothing more; naturally the sooner the better, lest a long night breed many dreams."

All that needed a word had had it; taking leave of Mr. Xu, I went with Brother Bingxi and sat a while, severally, at the lodgings of the two Brothers Cao Shi'ang and Tan Tianqian, meaning likewise to give them a word. Though I did not say it out to either of them, I dropped some hints. Brother Tan Tianqian sat wooden, as with a knot of care he could not undo—he had, I think, not caught my meaning. Brother Cao Shi'ang, charged from the first with a like mission, took the point at a touch, and of his own accord declared his hope that I would assign him a fitting task for him to undertake; the more so as his French wife had long since promised to shirk no peril and was very willing to lend a heart and a hand. I was deeply moved; only, having no such plan in mind, I could but ask him to let me think it over more, and, if there were truly some part where I might lean on him, answer him then.

Parting from Brother Bingxi, I went back alone to my quarters, and at once called together the three—Luqiao, Jiansheng, and Fengyi—to settle the date and hour of setting out and a few main principles, and in the end resolved on the following three points:

Before the twenty-second of March, one last reconnaissance was to be made; Tang Yingjie was again designated to go out, and Wei Chunfeng and the rest would re-survey from the side of the local police detectives, so that the two might be checked against each other.

If the result of the reconnaissance showed no great change from what had been understood before, then execution would be set for eleven o'clock on the night of the twenty-second of March; barring some change in the situation, this would not be altered again;
Upon entering Wang's residence, all action would be commanded by Luqiao, seconded and continued by Jiansheng, with Luqiao as the principal, to carry out the sanction task.

When we had settled our counsel, I sent Zhang Fengyi to fetch Tang Yingjie; but he was not at home. I asked Luqiao, who said too that he had not come to say anything, and that he did not know where he had run off to. It was past noon before Tang Yingjie came back; I upbraided him for slipping out on his own without reporting, but he said it was because his stomach ached and he had gone out to buy some medicine and come straight back, and had not meant to walk to several shops without finding any, so was delayed. This was plainly a lie, yet there was no help for it. I told him what we had just settled, and asked him to go out once more that night to reconnoiter the goings-on at the Wang house, paying particular heed to whether Wang's daily quarters had already been shifted. I earnestly begged him again to take much pains and do it thoroughly and truly—best to choose a spot with cover, stay as long as he could, and quietly observe the whole of it. Tang Yingjie nodded to signify he took it, turned, and went, saying he must go and have a good sleep.

Thereupon I detailed Zhang Fengyi to keep him company, to find a chance to talk him round out of his sulks, and at the same time charged Zhang Fengyi to go along with him that night as patrol and cover.

That day, the nineteenth of March, passed particularly long; uneasy in mind, and fretting too over Tang Yingjie's reconnaissance, I did not sleep sound the whole night. Before daybreak, Yingjie and Fengyi, the two of them, came quietly back; they had meant to wait and make their report after I rose, but seeing me just then coming out of the bedroom, there was no need to wait longer. Yingjie said: "I have been; it was done under Zhang Fengyi's oversight. I stayed a long while on the rooftop, and there was not a stir; the one still lit at night is that room on the third floor—there is no mistake, he lodges on the third floor." As I took in Tang Yingjie's report, I watched, on the other side, the look in Zhang Fengyi's eyes; he wore no peculiar expression—such as a faint smile, a wink of the eye, or the like. So it was proved that Tang Yingjie's report was true, and my mind was much the easier for it. It is not that I did not trust a comrade; in a matter so grave, I believe Tang Yingjie himself would not have dared, out of sloth, to lie; only that, some untrue things in his past history being what they were, I could not but add an extra grain of care.
Tang Yingjie went off to sleep, and Zhang Fengyi too made ready to rest. I fixed my eyes on Zhang Fengyi once more; he made no response—which was to say he had nothing to tell me.
And so I settled it that Wang lodged in that bedroom on the third floor of No. 27 Gao Lang Street—and this was the last pointer to our imminent action!

The next day, the twentieth of March of the twenty-eighth year, was a day never to be forgotten. In the morning, about half past nine, just as the three of us—I, Luqiao, and Jiansheng—were at the dining table going over Tang Yingjie's reconnaissance report, Wei Chunfeng came running in alone from outside to tell me: "The Wang house is packing its luggage; it looks as if the whole family is going out—I don't yet know where." Not a minute or two later, Mr. Xu too telephoned word: "He is preparing, with his household, to set out before noon for Da Le; whether to stay there a few days, or to turn by way of Saigon and put to sea from there, is not yet clear." The two pieces of news, though from different sources, tallied fairly well; taking them for ground and adding a little inference, one could all but judge that Wang and his whole family were about to leave Hanoi. Yet there was still something puzzling in it: Da Le, I understood, was a summer resort, a good few hours' journey from Hanoi; and this being only early spring, what would he go there for? And Da Le lay halfway from Hanoi to Saigon—was he then not coming back? Had some word leaked and startled him?

Because time pressed—there was in fact no time left to verify—I had to decide at once and take the proper steps without delay; that was the right course. Yet I could not help hesitating a little; not that I doubted the news itself, reliable or no, but that, in this sudden turn beyond all our reckoning, what was to be done?
I took no further counsel with them; silent a moment, and turning it over a while—as though I had fallen into a brief daze—I then made the following decision:

Wang Luqiao and Yu Jiansheng were to pass the word, each his way, and at once call together the comrades Zhang Fengyi, Tang Yingjie, Chen Bangguo, and Chen Buyun; each to carry his weapon and gear, to muster and await orders, ready to set out.

Wei Chunfeng was charged to go back and get in touch with the local employed hands, and—under the requirement of leaving no trace—to keep watch near Wang's residence, and, whatever movement he might spy, to telephone word with all speed.

Fang Bingxi was to be notified by telephone to go at once and stay close by Mr. Xu, asking him to contrive, through his private connections with the Hanoi police authorities, to learn Wang's movements at any moment and inform us.

After that, Luqiao and I went out the door to check over that two-door Ford sedan—filled it up with fuel and tried the engine. Taking this spare moment of checking the car, Luqiao and I made a few suppositions together about the many problems soon to face us; I remember I once said to Luqiao: "What comes after—that rests wholly on you now."

A little after ten in the morning, Wei Chunfeng telephoned back from outside; unchanged in his old habit, he said, still slow and deliberate: "Two big black sedans have driven off from the front gate of the Wang house; if I judge rightly, by the look of it they are heading toward the Red River bridge." Then he added: "I see them—there are a lot of people, the husband and wife both among them." One could gather that he was watching the other party's movements closely even as he telephoned, and reporting offhand.

This call happened to be one I took myself; the time did not allow of much asking; my reaction at the moment was, in instinct, the one word "Chase!" So I gave the order aloud, bade them take up their weapons and all get into the car at once. The car was small; counting me, seven of us in all were seated in it, among them one especially big man and two of the largest size; and though we split three in front and four behind, it was still packed full—passers-by, seeing it, found it truly out of the common.
What if we met a policeman who stopped and questioned us? That was a thing thought of only afterward; at the time there was no room at all to mind such a thing happening.

The writer drove; pressed close on my left was Luqiao; on the outside, next the door, was the tall, big-framed Chen Bangguo; Fengyi, Jiansheng, Yingjie, and Buyun were in the back seat—Fengyi and Jiansheng, the two being burly, took a supine posture, their backs against the rear cushion; Yingjie and Buyun, being shorter, leaned their heads forward, and rather than say they sat, one had better say they half-crouched, half-straddled across the legs of Fengyi and Jiansheng. I knew the way toward the Red River bridge, for it was a most conspicuous landmark, far too famous thereabouts—a pity only that in the ordinary way I had never thought to go and take a look at it.

As we went, in the car no one spoke; perhaps it was because I alone kept silent, so that none of them cared to open his mouth. I believe that at such a moment even the most composed of men would feel tension in some degree, chiefly not from any fear of hardship, but from a kind of suspense over the unknown. Even I, the commander, apart from the pursuit, could not tell just what we were to make ready to do; that must wait until we had caught up before anything could be decided; for the present it was but a "supposing," and what was there to say of it?

The car reached the head of the Red River bridge, and there, as luck would have it, the bridge deck was under repair, so that all vehicles coming and going could pass on a single lane only; happily, our car had just caught the green light. The vehicles fell into a line, nose to tail, and crept forward. The traffic warden did indeed cast several glances at us, but happily made no sign. To cross a single bridge cost a full ten-odd minutes—it was maddening. Once over the deck, the approach on this side curved a little; when we had reached the straight, we opened the throttle wider, passed several cars in a row, and sped on.

After going a stretch, looking far off, at a distance of some eight or nine hundred metres there were two big black sedans stopped on a patch of open ground by the road; though one could not see clearly, since it was just two big sedans, might this not be the Wang family's party?

We pushed forward again about four or five hundred metres; the first thought was to slow the car and find a place to stop, so as to observe and judge more easily at a nearer distance. So we halted at about three hundred metres from the cars ahead. I charged the comrades in the car not to get out and move about for the time, lest we draw the other party's notice.

That day the sky was clear for ten thousand li, the visibility very high; I saw that those two cars by the road both had their fronts squared to the roadway and stood side by side, unmoving. This was easy enough to read: nothing but to keep themselves free to advance or retreat together, and handy either way; but as to what people sat inside the cars, that could not be made out.

Setting my mind and looking across again, only on the one car I could see was there, in the front seat, a man showing an arm; the rear window-glass was not rolled down, and there was the sun's reflection besides, so that truly nothing could be seen.

Time slips by in an instant, the situation still unclear, and the fret of one's mind may be imagined. I listened to what all thought, and again each had his own notion, and I knew not whose to follow. By Chen Bangguo's account, in those two cars must be the fellow himself, and we ought to charge straight up, draw and fire, and talk after it was done. Yu Jiansheng patted Chen Bangguo on the shoulder and called to him not to run wild, then said to me: "It is safer to make out first just what people are in the cars, and then decide the next step." I thought there was much sense in it, and was just about to start the engine and drive over, when Chen Buyun, who sat in the back row and never spoke, spoke up: "We must beware there are Annamese police detectives on their cars guarding them!" Right—his saying so truly put me on my guard; whether by their own act or another's, it was in fact a possibility, and we could not but take care; for should we by mischance do a hurt to the local police, not only would the thing be botched, but there would come about a pass past all mending! At this there was no leisure for more discussion; I trod the throttle and drove toward the two cars still standing there, resolved to graze past in front of them and seize the chance to see clearly and for certain.
At the time the car ran too fast; I had to hold the wheel and could not well turn my head to look, but I kept prompting them from my mouth: "Mind—look sharp."

See we did; but because it was a flash of a scan, like light skimming a surface, it was truly not clear enough. Still, of what we wanted to know we had already the greater part, namely this: on the two cars, drivers included, there were nine or ten persons in all, of whom we knew only three—apart from the couple Wang Jingwei and Chen Bijun, there was one Zeng Zhongming; the rest we did not know at all. As for which were attendant bodyguards, and whether there were local plainclothes detectives guarding him—that, of course, could not be settled by one glance; but Luqiao and Jiansheng and the others said all with one voice: "Those few don't look like detectives…" The words were not out before our car had passed several dozen metres; someone looked back—the two cars stopped there had begun to move; and of a sudden Bangguo cried out: "Turn round quick—they've run for it." I braked hard, and by the time I had swung the car about, the cars ahead had already sped away!

I could not clearly hear who it was that, unable to wait, was shouting "Chase!"; oddly enough, at that moment what I was thinking too was just "Chase!" I had a mind to chase to within effective range and then give the order to fire!

Their cars, ranged fore and aft—the one bearing Wang in front, the other following—were faster than ours; by eye the distance was over two hundred metres, and still stretching longer. I reckoned roughly this did not much matter: once at the bridgehead, the car in front would surely slow; though the two might not touch nose to tail, they would not be too far apart either, and then one could see more truly. Thinking so, I weighed it in my own mind: if there were a chance at the bridge's edge, should we act? No—cars before and behind, no way to break off the scene; then on the bridge itself? Worse still—short of being taken with our hands bound, there was no luck to be had; the best choice was after crossing the bridge…. Just then there was a horn behind, and a car passed us; by the look of it, it meant to overtake the cars ahead too, but swaying left and right, it found no gap, could by no means get past, and ended jammed in the middle—right in our way.

In a twinkling we were at the bridge's edge; who could have looked for coincidence on coincidence—or else the luck was too bad—for just as we watched Wang's two cars pass through, and it came to the turn of the car in front of us, the light flashed and turned red. Meeting such a thing, one could neither hurry nor fume; there was nothing for it but to hold one's temper and wait—unless one could fly across the Red River bridge? All were silent; the big fellow Chen Bangguo spoke up again: "I said charge up and be done with it—how much simpler; isn't this just asking for trouble?" True enough: too much caution, and wavering, are what spoil a thing. But this was no time to reckon gains and losses; though we had lost the first move, we could not own ourselves beaten for that, and must find another chance to come again—that was the right course.

The light changed to green; the car ahead drove very fast, and as the bridge deck was rough and uneven, seen from behind it seemed to bob and leap; our own car went far more smoothly. Over the bridge, and a stretch on, the car ahead was already out of sight; pressing on, there was a fork, and I resolved to turn into the one running through the busy quarter, by which one could cut a nearer way to Gao Lang Street—chiefly because there was still, after all, a little hope of catching them up.

Coming to a crossroads in the commercial district, we met a red light again; it was just then the midday rest, and the vehicles on the road were especially thick. Stopping the car and gazing far off, I unexpectedly found that the two big black sedans we meant to pursue were also stopped at the crossing—only, there was still a good stretch between us, and at the time I had no heart to count how many car-lengths; think of it, surely more than ten cars? This, then, was a thing one might look at but not come at!

It was not that the thought did not come—that if one could now but swing the car about, one might well go by another road, round in front of them, and, catching them off guard, deal a head-on blow; and then, in the fright and confusion of the passers-by, it would not be easy to break off the scene and withdraw in safety—yet this was not without its chance; the pity was that the road was choked with cars, and, caught in a strait between advance and retreat, we could not stir.

There was no help for it but to trail along behind. Sure enough, those two cars did return to Gao Lang Street. This bootless chase came to nothing—labor spent going and coming, and home again with clipped wings. Nor was that the worst; the greatest harm was that we had now given away our identity and our design, so that from this time on they were bound to sharpen their vigilance and strengthen their guard, which by the same measure made the execution of our task the harder still.
In this passage of events there is one great riddle that not only can the writer not explain, but to which there will never again be any answer! Readers may just be about to ask:
Where exactly was Wang's party bound?
Why stop by the road once over the bridge? What did they stop there for?
Was it that, finding themselves followed, they turned back to Hanoi? Or was there some other cause?
On these several points the writer truly does not know; to answer would be all guesswork, and I had best leave it to the reader to guess for himself!

In October of the thirtieth year of the Republic, when the writer met with disaster and was arrested at Shanghai, Wang's wife Chen Bijun, in the questioning, raised no few matters; thinking of it now—why did I not, at the time, put these questions back to her, and so untie the knot of doubt that had lain pent in my heart these many years?

When we all came back from the Red River bridge, our vexation was at its height; we wished neither to rest nor to eat, nor even to say much at all. What each of them was thinking I do not know; but as for me, the more I thought, the more wretched I felt, and I could not shake a sense of shame beyond the common.

This passage of events, explain it how one might, could not escape the reproach of ill handling; and to win back what was already lost—no matter whether the situation would change—there was nothing for it but to fight for time and press on the harder. That is to say, if we did not act with all speed, the chances, I feared, would be few, and the difficulty the greater. What was past all mending was that we had "beaten the grass and startled the snake"; it seemed one might take it as certain that the other party had already found out our identity and our design.
The mind being made up, there was no need for much counsel; and what was now most of all wanted was just this one thing—intelligence of Wang's movements.

Because it did not do to say much on the telephone, I asked Luqiao to go and bring Wei Chunfeng; and at the same time got in touch with Brother Bingxi, asking him to keep still in contact with Mr. Xu, and, so far as might be, to learn all he could of Wang's movements, and, better still, to pass it on to me at any moment.

By now it was past noon; Luqiao, Chunfeng, and Miss Nguyen, the three of them, came in together. I asked Miss Nguyen to sit a while downstairs, drew Wei Chunfeng up to the upper floor, and told him straight out the course of the pursuit of Wang just now, then at once asked him to use every means he could to fasten upon the Wang household's every move, and, whatever he might find, to tell me at any time; if that Miss Nguyen could help, nothing could be better—leave it to you to entrust it to her. As for … here I could say no more—this too is the way of my temper; all my life I have never liked, at just such a pinch, to make promises; and the reverse is the same, for if a man, when he has come to the point of needing me, then comes out with a set of honeyed words, that only stirs my distaste the more.

How clever was Wei Chunfeng; without waiting for me to say more, he declared resolutely: "So far as my strength reaches, I will surely do my utmost; if only I may serve the nation, I ask for nothing at all." Good! This pure-hearted young man was truly worthy of respect. I said no more, but asked him to hurry and get in touch with those people, looking to him for report on report.
We seven still kept in a state of combat readiness.

At four o'clock that afternoon, Wei Chunfeng telephoned; in a hurried tone he told me: "The two of them, husband and wife, are standing just now on the lawn outside the door, talking—it looks as if they're arguing over something. What do you think we should do?" I told him: "You go off first; I'll come and see."

I at once called together Luqiao and Fengyi to set out with me, bade the rest await assignment, named Jiansheng to be in charge; the arranging done, we ran to the car and drove straight for Gao Lang Street. In the car, recalling the telephone just now, it seemed a thing that could hardly happen: in these two months and more, we had never once seen him show himself before the door; how, after taking a fright, should he on the contrary come out to the door to "make an appearance" with no fear at all? This was a strange thing indeed—were we ourselves being oversensitive? Was it that they had as yet no sense of our pursuit? The road took at most only five minutes; but by the time we hurried up, there was not a soul before the door; not far off, at the mouth of a little lane, a "plainclothesman" was pacing about, and besides that nothing at all. Looking again at that great door, shut fast, it was no different from the scene we had always seen.

This trip, too, drew a blank! The first time, the trip to the Red River bridge, we had let a good chance slip and chased to no purpose, coming home crestfallen; this second time, in a mood of self-reproach, I could not but feel some remorse again. With so many of us, I thought—rather than leave them idle and unused, why not adopt a mobile method, and keep a three-man team always posted near Wang's residence, watching close, keeping watch by turns; so that, meeting such a case as just now, one might strike on the instant, at any time; and though this were a little more toilsome, the odds of success would be much the greater. Was it a hundred cares and one slip? A minding of this and a losing of that? Or was "take counsel and then move" too much by rote?

Matters having come to this pass—two fine chances already slipped—among the seven of us most were unwilling to take it lying down; one might describe it as fired up: though they had not lost their reason, there was a strain of feeling in it. I announced that, having begun, we would not stop halfway, and resolved, come what might, to make a surprise assault, storming the place that very night.

At eleven forty on the night of the twentieth of March, the same seven men, in the deep hush of the night, set quietly out. I believe the heart of every one of us was very heavy. I have heard men boast that to hear of a killing is a joy like a child's in new shoes; unless a man be mad and lost to conscience, that is all rubbish—not to speak of others, take my own case: if it were for myself, I should not dare go at all. These were, to be sure, two idle words, and might as well be left unsaid. To go on: before we set out, the several of us had already been assigned our parts, the division of duties as follows:
The writer himself—direction and command;

Wang Luqiao, Yu Jiansheng, Chen Bangguo, and Tang Yingjie, four men, to enter the residence, with Chen Bangguo named the vanguard to open the road—big and strong of body, brave and fierce, he was well fit to bear this heavy charge; Tang Yingjie to follow close on Chen Bangguo and guide them up the stairs—having gone several times before to reconnoiter, he was to be reckoned an old horse that knew the way, and could surely make no error; Wang Luqiao principal and Yu Jiansheng second, the two to carry out the rooting-out of the traitor together, backing and covering each other; Zhang Fengyi and Chen Buyun to patrol without doors, as sentries.
Before setting out, it had been arranged with Wei Chunfeng that he would take charge of close liaison with the local employed hands, and keep in touch with me at any time and place.
For this sally, I again drove the car myself—for one thing, it could serve as a lead; and secondly, it could, without one's knowing it, steady the feelings.

As we went, I warned them again and again, on no account to forget that old saying, "the guilt reaches not to wife and child"; besides the target man, they must do no hurt to any other. Whether this ran counter to that guiding maxim, "nothing short of a great bloodletting will strike terror into the enemy's heart," I truly did not think of at the time—perhaps it did not apply in a case like this?

A few turns and we had driven near Wang's residence; our car had just stopped in a lane on the left side of Gao Lang Street, and Luqiao and the others had not all yet jumped down, when of a sudden two Annamese plainclothes detectives came up out of the dark to our faces; they jabbered something we none of us could understand, and then made signs, gesturing a good while, before we grasped that they meant we were not to stop here and must be off quick. This, though a thing not to be resisted, yet blocked our next move; just at this strait between advance and retreat, Wei Chunfeng appeared like timely rain—asking nothing much, he drew one detective off into the dark, and the other followed too; what they muttered I do not know; in a little Wei Chunfeng nodded to me and ran over, and asked whether I had money on me. Without a thought I felt in my pocket, pulled it out, and thrust it into Wei Chunfeng's hand; he counted it—4,500 in all, five hundred to a note, nine notes—and saying in his mouth, "Let them have it all," turned and went back to deal with the two. I stood there dazed, unable for the moment to take it in.

This thing was too incredible; had I not gone through it in my own person, say it how one would, it would be hard to believe; and yet it was the plain and certain truth. Only in that age, in that region, and with the sort of men we met, could such a thing have come to pass.

Wei Chunfeng came back very soon, and said they had been "sent packing." At that I breathed a sigh of relief, yet gained a few more cares thereby. They were, after all, only some low-ranking detectives; though charged with guarding the Wang house, they could never have guessed what we were about to do; for the moment, coveting that little gain, they had merely got out of sight a while, and, with no need for much verifying, it was a certain thing that they still lurked in the dark, spying. Though I knew this well, yet, driven by the situation—was I, after all, to shrink back and give it up? Heedless of everything, we resolved to go on with the plan as fixed!

As was said before, Gao Lang Street lies in a high-class residential quarter within the city of Hanoi, the surroundings quiet and elegant; No. 27, Wang's residence, faced a tree-lined avenue, old banyans standing thick in clumps, great royal palms towering to the clouds—by rights a fair tropical scene; but at this moment the boughs and leaves of the banyans and the palms, stretching and swaying without cease in the night wind, were like demon-shadows and monster-hands, and lent instead a grim and eerie air.

On this great street, not to speak of the dead of night, even in broad day the passers-by were often few and the carriages and horses scarce. No. 27 was a three-story building, and the houses near it were all high-class residences of the same style. This house occupied a single side—that is, on one side were dwellings, on the other a lane. Going along the lane toward the rear, there was a low wall; low, one calls it, but it was in fact higher than a man; and within the wall was a small courtyard—this was the back yard of No. 27.

The back yard had a door, always kept shut, seldom used in the ordinary way, and no doubt bolted. To break it open, if we made ready to, would of course be no hard thing; but there was no way to do it without noise, and any noise would startle them. So the plan was to send one man in first, and then open the door from within; this too was not wholly safe, but far better, on the whole.

The one fittest to take this charge was, of course, Tang Yingjie. Wang Luqiao led the party to the wall's foot; Tang Yingjie, first of all, raised both hands high, gripped the wall-top, and vaulted over; when he came down inside the yard, there was truly not a sound. He had meant to open the back door from within; but feeling it over, it was not only bolted—outside the bolt a great lock had been added besides; a hard wrench, and it did not give a hair's breadth; seeing it would not do, he hastily thrust out his head to signal. Then Chen Bangguo took the lead, and with both feet on Zhang Fengyi's shoulders climbed over the wall; at the same time Wang Luqiao and Yu Jiansheng too were hoisted up, one by one, by Chen Buyun. After that, Zhang Fengyi kept guard outside the back door, and Chen Buyun ranged between the lane and the street, the two keeping answer to each other.

The little courtyard within the back door was no more than five metres square; there was another small door leading to the adjoining side, which for the time they took no note of. Up three steps was the door giving on the back court; only by entering this door could one mount the stairs and go within. Chen Bangguo first pressed the door with his palm, meaning to test its material and how stoutly it was made; then he turned the knob, and, sure enough, it was shut fast; without much more thought, he drew from his waist a hatchet made ready beforehand, and with hacking and hewing and a fierce kick of his foot, it flew open with a crash. Needless to say, this burst of great noise, and in the dead of night, was bound to have startled greatly all the household of the Wang house, high and low—only that they were not to be seen.

Wang Luqiao, his spirit like a rainbow, without waiting for Tang Yingjie to lead the way, weapon in hand, sprang up the stairs at a flying step; Tang Yingjie and Yu Jiansheng followed close on Luqiao and mounted the stairs one after another.

Chen Bangguo, changing from attack to defense, stayed on the ground floor, to cover the safety of those gone up and at the same time to keep the way out. Setting his mind, he searched around, and of a sudden found a man push open a door, poke out his head, and steal a look outward; in the stress of the moment he raised his gun and fired, loosing several shots in a row toward that door, and bawling from his mouth: "Come out again and I'll really let you have it." Whether it caused death or wound at the time no one knew; but it did press the other party down, and he drew back at once.

A few reports of gunfire broke the night's stillness; I, sitting in the car, was, I suppose, the most keenly alive to it. I moved the car to another position, and looked toward that direction of No. 27—not a stir; looking round about too, no shadow of a man; and just as I was guessing at the cause of the shots just now, there it was again—three more reports came. Once more I drove slow and easy, making ready to take them up and cover their withdrawal into the car. It was only at this point that it struck me all at once—why had I not thought beforehand to change the car's number-plate?
To speak now of the doings of Wang Luqiao and the others, up on the floors above.

Luqiao came at a flying step to the second floor; the electric lamp at the stairhead was still lit, but not a shadow of a man was to be seen, and the doors of the several rooms were all shut fast. Just as he was about to turn up to the third floor, of a sudden a young man came out from behind the staircase, and met Luqiao square, face to face; Luqiao, startled, at once looked him swiftly up and down: seeing his hands empty, his face full of fright, and that he was not the appointed target of the action, he was a little the more at ease, and gave the man a few motions with the muzzle of his gun, telling him in a low voice: "Don't cry out—get back quick," and, saying it, without minding what the man might do next, turned and strode up the flights to the third floor.

Luqiao reached the third floor, and, hand on the railing, glanced down below; Jiansheng was already standing at the stairhead of the second floor. Luqiao asked: "Did you see that man?" Jiansheng waved his hand. So Luqiao, having no care for his rear, at last with an easy and bold heart made for the main room to the right, near the front end.

This was the one we had reconnoitered beforehand, and had had Tang Yingjie lie hid on the roof and re-survey twice besides; so that in our minds we were certain this was Wang Jingwei's bedroom, where he passed his days.

Luqiao pushed the door; it would not move; he worked the handle again, and it would not turn either; one could be certain this door was bolted from within, which proved too that there must be someone in the room. Luqiao stepped back two paces and, borrowing that rush of force, gave it a kick—still it would not open. In his stress a shift came to him: he turned to the stairhead and signed to Yu Jiansheng to send up the hatchet quick; Jiansheng, taking his meaning, was just making ready to leap down for it when Tang Yingjie, quick as flying, had already brought the hatchet up to the third floor.
Jiansheng called Yingjie down to take his place at the guard-post, and himself came up to the third floor too.

Wang Luqiao and Jiansheng together hacked out a panel in the middle of the door, thrust in a hand and felt for the knob within, turned it several times, and still could find no way to get the door open—which made certain that the door was locked. By now a great hole a foot square had been opened in the door panel; Luqiao crouched down, tilted his head, and looked in: by the lamplight, he saw, under the bed, a man lying prone—and a big man at that. His upper body was hidden under the bed and could not be seen at all; his loins, back, and both legs were all bared without; no doubt, hearing the noise and knowing the alarm, in his sudden helplessness he had taken this way of hiding. Judging by the frame that could be seen, and with the fixed idea already in mind, who could this be but Wang Jingwei?
It was under these circumstances that Luqiao, on the instant, made his judgment—the man lying prone under the bed was Wang Jingwei.

Luqiao, without the least hesitation, raised his gun and fired, loosing three shots in a row; and because the distance was too close, he saw each and every bullet go into the back and loins of the man under the bed. The one thing Comrade Luqiao took for a lasting regret was that he could not get the door open, and so had no way to drag the man out and see for certain who he was.

Between these two bursts of gunfire there was an interval of no more than four or five minutes, but I already felt I had been circling the streets a very, very long time. What most left me uneasy was—did they meet with trouble, or were they held up? Or had they carried the task through without a hitch?

I gave my whole mind to marking their traces; and on the other hand had to beware the sudden appearance of the detectives. I looked at my watch—it was now past midnight, reckoned nine minutes past the zero hour of the second day. Lifting my head, I saw a plainclothesman standing at the lane-mouth wave to me again and again, meaning that I should get away quick—perhaps he took me for a "passer-by." I paid him no heed; still, I got clear of his sight as fast as I could, and went on circling nearby. In this way, another two or three minutes or so were spent, when of a sudden I found Luqiao, alone, both hands thrust in his trouser pockets, turning out of a little lane; I hastily braked, and, on purpose, let out a "screech" of sound, to call him into the car—though in fact he had seen me long before.

Luqiao and I circled slow once more, hoping to take up the other comrades; but not one was to be seen. I thought—it might be that, because my car kept moving, they could not find it for the moment, and the case being urgent they could not wait long; nor need they wait for the car at all; very likely they were each seeking a safe way out on his own and going back to the quarters. Just at this moment, two police cars, large and small, bearing a great troop of armed police, came racing and roaring up—for the thing that had just happened, of course. Luqiao and I, knowing well we could stay no longer, had to drive from the scene in time and go back to our lodging. We took great care, too, that none should be following.

There was no waiting to be back before speaking; on the road, Luqiao told me: "The thing is done; I watched three shots go into Wang's loins, his two legs gave a few twitches and then stirred no more, his whole body curled under the bed. What is wanting is only that I never got to see his face."

I was overjoyed to hear it, and for a spell felt a lightness as of a burden set down; this was the happiest moment I had known since I took up the charge of this case—and if you ask how long it lasted, it may have been but two seconds.
Set these two seconds against several decades, and they are utterly out of all proportion, long against short; and of men who meet with such a thing in life there are, I think, not many.

Luqiao and I, come safe back to the quarters, he first went and washed his face, cleaning off the grime; I drank a cup of cold boiled water, to pour a little on the fire in my heart. The two of us sat face to face without a word, and fell silent, our whole minds only on the hope that the five—Jiansheng and the rest—would come back the sooner. I turned over too, meanwhile, the matter of making report to our superiors; this, I thought, must not be hurried, and it were more fitting to wait till all were gathered, to hear out their whole account and get the certain result, and then send the telegram.

After seven or eight minutes, Tang Yingjie and Chen Buyun, the two of them, came back one after the other; they had come by different ways and had no contact with each other; waiting on, not one more was to be seen. We waited right on to past four o'clock before dawn, and still there was no word, no more men came back. Chen Buyun proposed that he go out and look; I thought it quite needless—whoever was to come back would come back, and where was one to go to look now? At this moment, what the situation outside was we knew nothing at all of; ill-managed, it might on the contrary spoil things; better a stillness than a stir—best to let it cool a while.

I thought to the good side—clinging, of course, to a hope; and I thought to the bad side too: Zhang Fengyi had never gone in at all; Yu Jiansheng and Chen Bangguo had come out together with Luqiao, and could by no means have taken hurt—had they, then, been seized by the police on the road?

At this moment I longed for Wei Chunfeng to telephone, but that telephone too seemed to have fallen asleep. When it came to about four fifty, the telephone rang; I still supposed it was Yu and Zhang and the rest calling, or else surely Wei Chunfeng; but lifting the receiver to listen, it proved to be Mr. Xu's voice, and he said, head-on: "You have got it wrong! That man is quite safe and sound; the one hurt is Zeng Zhongming…" The writer, hearing this far, had no heart to hear more; it was verily like missing one's footing from a tower ten thousand feet high—my whole body went cold, and I felt it first go cold from the heart, and then, following the round of the blood, my hands and feet turned icy too, till at last I stiffened where I stood, without even the strength to speak.

Luqiao, not knowing the inside of it, asked me what the matter was; fearing he would take a shock, and unwilling to make him ill at ease to hear it, I said only, lightly: "A wrong number." Luqiao, hearing it, said nothing for a good while; then all at once, as if something had dawned on him, he slapped his thigh, showed a spare valor yet to spend, and, as though to comfort me, said: "It's all right—we'll do it again!"

I answered with a wry smile, signifying that this too was just my mind; and while my heart was even then sketching the possibility and the practicability of another attempt, Mr. Xu telephoned again to say: "Three men have been taken!" This was one more douche of cold water poured over my head.
Mr. Xu's word was past all doubt; the thing being come to this, I could only bow my head and accept the fact, and, the more, with a strong will bear this heavy blow on blow.

See the complete translation of "The Secret Records of President Chiang," Volume Eleven, page 203, where it is set down: "On the twenty-first of March, Zeng Zhongming, secretary to Wang Zhaoming, was slain by patriotic men of resolve at Wang's hidden residence on Gao Lang Street in Hanoi." "For it happened that on just this one night Wang Zhaoming had by chance changed his sleeping-room; the assassins mistook Zeng Zhongming for Wang himself, and fired several shots into the room."

"At this time, the moneys Wang Zhaoming carried were all deposited in the bank in Zeng's name; and so the gravely wounded and dying Zeng Zhongming propped himself up to sit and, on his sickbed, signed every one of the cheques, whereby he lost too much blood and died."

According to the explanation of the Japanese "Sankei Shimbun," which published "The Secret Records of President Chiang," this material was furnished by the Party History Committee of the Chinese Nationalist Party. This is a semi-official record, and must of course have had its grounds.

In "The Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong," published by the Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense in October of the sixty-eighth year of the Republic (the "Complete Works of Mr. Dai Yunong" being wholly identical with it), in the tenth section, "Discerning the Loyal from the Rebel; Rooting Out Traitors at Hanoi" (from page ninety-four), there is likewise a passage of record, whereof I here excerpt a few paragraphs of the original text, as follows:

"Mr. Dai in person inspected the terrain of the airfields and harbor, made clear the inner circumstances of Wang's residence, appointed special men to reconnoiter Wang's movements, and secretly laid inside lines in the Vietnamese public and private offices in touch with Wang; he designated Chen Gongshu as work-group leader, charged with carrying out the traitor-rooting task. The disposition complete, he first returned to Chongqing.

"Wang's residence at Hanoi, on Rue Colombert, was a stout and imposing building, with high walls all round, wire mesh set atop the walls; without the door were Vietnamese police and plainclothesmen on guard, within the door Wang's own guards in constant attendance; and Wang himself kept the door shut all day and did not go out—so that how to get at him cost no little perplexity.

"On the twentieth of March, Chen got word that Wang, taking only two policemen and his personal guards, had ridden in a black sedan bearing plate number (39) to the town of Dan Dao, ninety kilometres from Hanoi, meaning to rest at a French hotel. Thereupon Chen and the rest divided into three parties, rode in three sedans, and drove at speed for Dan Dao. But midway they found that Wang's car had already returned from Dan Dao to Hanoi; so they hurriedly turned back in pursuit, and saw very clearly Wang seated in his car. Just as they were making ready to overtake and cut him off, of a sudden the great bridge, three kilometres long, that spans the Red River was before their eyes. Because of road repairs, vehicles could pass on a single lane only. Wang's car, reaching the bridgehead, was stopped by a red light; Chen and the rest, in their joy, got down from their cars in a flurry, meaning to hurry up and pick him off. But because there were still many other vehicles stopped ahead, to go past on foot needed a stretch of time. By the time they were nearing Wang's car, Wang's guards had very alertly dashed through the changing red light and driven at speed over the bridge. Chen and the rest hurried to their car and drove over the bridge, but there was no way to trail him and get at him.

"The several attempts having failed, Wang had perhaps taken warning; and this affair could on no account be longer delayed; so Chen and the rest resolved that 'without entering the tiger's den, how shall one get the tiger's cub,' and with a resolve to spare no cost, however great the sacrifice, went straight to Wang's residence in the small hours of the twenty-first. First they contrived to lure away the guards outside the wall; then Wang Luqiao and four others, five men in all, climbed the wall, broke the mesh, and got within, killed Wang's inner-court guard, and swiftly sprang upstairs; according to the inner circumstances of Wang's residence understood beforehand, they made in haste for Wang's third-floor bedroom, broke through the closed door, and, with all the lamps put out, by the light of a flashlight shot dead one man in a white shirt.
