At this the Vietnamese police without the door blew hard on their whistles; the neighbors right and left, startled awake by the gunfire, raised the alarm on every side; the guard dogs in the yard, too, broke their leashes and bayed, seeking the 'foe'; Wang and the rest, holding their task accomplished, did not care to linger and search out the others, but made an urgent withdrawal. In the end, three men—Yu Jiansheng, Zhang Fengyi, and Chen Bangguo—were nonetheless captured, and were sentenced by the Vietnamese authorities to seven years' imprisonment."

The "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission" of the twenty-eighth year of the Republic (styled in brief the "Juntong Bureau" or the "Juntong") was the forerunner of what is now the "Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense." The archival records of all major cases are likewise kept by the Intelligence Bureau.

The several passages of record quoted above were, of course, compiled on the ground of the archives. Only, the incidents and content they describe cannot, in detail, but differ a little from what was written in the earlier part of the present text.
What I write is wholly from my own memory;
What is set down in "The Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong" is grounded on the preserved archives.

On this question the writer once talked with a retired business chief of the Intelligence Bureau, in the winter of the seventieth year, and he said: "The 'Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong' published by the Intelligence Bureau, though it does not stand for an 'official document,' has yet the character of an 'official record.'"

To speak of it, this is a matter of much interest and no little savor: if the record in "The Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong" is finer than what I wrote in the book "The Full Story of the Wang Case at Hanoi," with more of the spirit of daring and braving peril—would that not be all the better?

Writing to this point, I once more laid down my pen and lay back, shut my eyes, and called up the former scene; think how I might, I could not recall whether I had ever put in a written report, and I remember too that Mr. Dai and I never once spoke again of this unhappy business. And so the less would any record have been left of it.

Whether Luqiao made any written report, or any record of an oral one, I truly do not know. From the thirty-seventh year at Tianjin, right on to our coming to Taiwan in the thirty-eighth year, and up to before his death, Luqiao and I met I know not how many times; but neither of us was ever willing to speak again of the Hanoi affair.
As for those who took part in the actual action—Yu Jiansheng, Zhang Fengyi, Chen Bangguo, Tang Yingjie, Chen Buyun, and the rest—whether they made reports afterward, I do not know either.

Brother Fang Bingxi, who knew of it but did not take part in the actual action, very likely made a fairly full written report, for I guess he bore an "inspectorate" charge besides; whether it were so, though, I dare not say for certain.

The other few comrades—Brother Cen Jiazhuo, Brother Yu Lexing, and so on—each having his own post of duty, took no part in the direct action; and even had they made reports, these would be fragmentary, and would not have described much of the state of the scene.

The point of all these trifling words is to make plain that I do not know just what material there may be in the archives now on file; could I but have a look at it, I should not have to guess blindly. Someone may perhaps ask: "Why not request that the file be called up for a reading?" By my understanding, there seems to be no such "rule," and so it is not convenient to entertain the thought.

Then why is what I write not wholly the same as what is on record? This is very hard to make plain in a word or two; forgive me a rough comparison, and it is this: "the assay is not pure"; "the coloring falsifies the truth."

The "Secret Records of President Chiang" and "The Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong" quoted above are both from our own side; let us look next at the side of Wang—is that not the better to widen the view? Of this kind of writing there is no little; and among it, "The Rise and Fall of the Wang Regime," written by Jin Xiongbai (pen name Zhu Zijia), is the more detailed.

"The Rise and Fall of the Wang Regime" was serialized from the forty-eighth year on in the magazine "Chunqiu" published at Hong Kong, and afterward came out in a separate edition. The original book was divided into six volumes in all, of which the fifth volume, from page forty-one to page forty-four, sets down the two episodes, "The Red River Pursuit" and "Midnight □□."

What he wrote must have had its sources; but one can see it was by no means told him from the Wangs' own mouths; whether he talked of the affair with someone among Wang's kin is a thing that should be possible. In what touches the inner circumstances of the Wang house, he knew more than I; in what touches the part of our action, he must of course yield to me; as for the incidents therein, they are half conjecture, and not without contradictions. His text is as follows:

"On the morning of the day before the murder, Wang still went out to San Tao Shan; hardly had he got there when the local police came hurrying to report that word abroad was pressing and grave, and bade Wang's people counsel him not to go out at will hereafter. On his way back to his residence, passing the Red River iron bridge, Wang got down from the car to rest, the police still following in guard. Later, as the car passed the Banque de l'Indochine, of a sudden a strange car came speeding by from behind, the men in it showing something odd in their looks; yet Wang remained unconcerned and thought nothing of it.

"No. 27 Gao Lang Street lies in a quiet corner of Hanoi. The house was of three stories. The ground floor: in front, the two large rooms left and right were both garages; the two rooms behind, adjoining, were servants' rooms; the staircase lay in the central part of the whole house. The middle floor: the two large rooms facing north, together with two small rooms on either side of the staircase, were all bedrooms of Wang's attendants; of the two rooms facing south, the front one was the drawing room, the back one the dining room. The top floor: to the left of the stairhead were two bathrooms, to the right two lavatories; of the two rooms facing north, the right was the bedroom of Miss Zhu Mei, second daughter of Zhu Zhixin, the left the bedroom of the couple Zeng Zhongming and Fang Junbi; of the two rooms facing south, the right was the bedroom of the couple He Wenjie and Wang Wenxing—which adjoined the room of Wang and his wife on its left; while Zeng Zhongming's bedroom was just opposite Wang's, and only a few feet apart.

"In the deep night of the twenty-first of March, about two o'clock, in the dead stillness, all in the house were asleep. Of a sudden someone came over the wall from the back garden and entered by the small back door; passing the ground-floor servants' rooms, an attendant, Dai Yunsheng, and the cook, He Jiu, hearing footsteps, opened their door to look, and the assailant, seeing them, at once fired: Dai Yunsheng took a bullet in the arm, He Jiu one each in leg and arm; another attendant, Chen Guoxing, hearing the shots, fled and hid under a car in the garage, and the ruffian fired one more shot, the cement fragments on the ground wounding his chest; then he mounted the stairs. In the room at the stairhead of the middle floor lodged Chen Guoqi, Wang's wife's nephew, who likewise came out at the noise; the assailant, meeting him head-on, fired one more shot, again hitting him in the leg, and forced him back into the neighboring room; then the assailant went up to the top floor. Miss Zhu was the first to hear the several intermittent reports of gunfire, and came out of her room to the stairhead to look; just then her neighbor Zeng Zhongming appeared at the same moment, and hearing a confused tramp of feet on the stairs, hastily pulled him back together into the bedroom, and quickly shut the door—but the assailant had already tracked them there. They hewed a hole in the wooden door of the room with a sharp axe, thrust the Mauser within—the weapon was a select-fire pistol able to fire in bursts—but happily Miss Zhu, on entering the room, had hidden just at the wall to the right of the door, precisely a dead angle beyond the reach of the bullets, and so was spared. But Zeng Zhongming and his wife stood before the bed, straight against the muzzle; at a press of the trigger the bullets loosed like a string of pearls, and Zhongming took wound on wound in loins and belly, thick as a honeycomb. His wife Fang Junbi took three bullets too—one in the arm, one in the leg, one in the right breast—and the two fell together into a pool of blood.

"By this time He Wenjie and his wife too had long been startled awake by the continuous, piercing gunfire! At first, at the few reports below, in their dreams they still doubted it for the sound of firecrackers; but afterward the volley fired into Zeng's room, close at hand, and in the dead stillness of deep night, made them feel that a great calamity had befallen at their very elbow. He and Miss Wenxing threw on their clothes and rose, and had just stepped out of their room-door when Wang too, hearing the noise, had come out. In a low voice he asked Wenjie: 'What is it?' Wenjie said vaguely: 'It is nothing,' and hastily pushed Wang back into the room. Thereupon Wang and his wife, and Wenxing, sat in the dark on the floor by the door against the wall. When Wang heard the heavy groaning that came from the couple Zhongming across the way, he several times made to rush the door and go out, but was each time held fast by Miss Wenxing. Had Wang come out of the room, he too would surely have met the poisoned hand; and had the assailants known that the room Wang lodged in was just opposite, they need but have turned about, and Wang and his wife would surely have followed the couple Zhongming. But the sound of the wounded couple Zhongming falling to the ground the assailants took for proof that they had struck Wang at a blow, and so in a flurry they went down the stairs and away.

"He Wenjie was the most fortunate of all: when he pushed Wang back into the bedroom, he did not yet know that the ones hurt were the couple Zeng Zhongming; so that, had he come out from Wang's room and walked toward Zhongming's room, he would have run just full into the assailants, their work done. But without meaning to, he first turned to the right, passed his own bedroom, then came to the stairhead and looked down: seeing on the middle floor a man reach out a hand to twist off the electric lamp, he found something amiss and drew back in haste, and returned by the way he came into Wang's room. After some thirty minutes in all had passed, the gunfire ceased and the assailants had, he judged, made off far; only then did Wenjie dare go to Zhongming's bedroom and push open the door: Miss Zhu was trembling behind the door, and the couple Zhongming had both fallen to the ground; putting out a hand to feel, it was wet and slippery—fresh blood ran over all the floor. In the faint light of the bedside lamp, he saw that half his own finger had been dyed red with the blood. The skirt and trousers over Miss Zhu's lower body, too, were spattered with bloodstains; and what lay before him was a scene so ghastly and dreadful!

"No one knows for certain just how many assailants went into the room. At the time of the deed, since within the Wang house all were bare-handed, without so much as a single gun for self-defense, they came and went as into a land of no men and could do as they pleased. At the doorways of the several bedrooms on the middle and lower floors, at the stairheads, at the windows, and all round without the house, there were men posted on watch, covering until the whole party had left; and only then did Wang's secretary, Wang Yi, cry wildly from a second-floor window toward the street: 'Help! Help!' Because Miss Zhu knew French, she went down, with He Wenjie attending her, to telephone the police. It was learned afterward that at that time the assailants still stayed openly in the back garden to spy out the movements within; and only when they heard Miss Zhu's voice calling for aid over the telephone, and he believed the aim accomplished, did they at their leisure go once more over the wall and away.

"Of the five wounded, Chen Guoqi was hurt in the leg and had himself bound the wound with a handkerchief; the attendants Dai Yunsheng and Chen Guoxing and the cook He Jiu were none of them badly hurt, and, given a first bandaging to keep from losing too much blood, stayed in the house to recover. When the ambulance reached the Wang house, it carried off only the couple Zeng Zhongming, the most gravely wounded, to the army hospital for treatment. Not until this hour did the Hanoi authorities send police to guard the Wang house on Gao Lang Street—and those who came were again but a few native local police, who, on arriving, had to be taught on the spot by a French police officer how to load cartridges and how to fire. Armed men who cannot so much as use their weapons—the 'guard' they gave was no more than a form." On this I will add a word of my own, and it is no idle cavil; but since the affair is long past, there is no need to add to the reader's tedium.

We spent no small pains on reconnaissance, and yet we never made out just how many people lived in that house, still less who was surnamed what or called what. For instance, that among them were Wang's daughter Wang Wenxing, his son-in-law He Wenjie, his wife's nephew Chen Guoqi, and so on—all this too was heard only afterward.

By what we knew, Zeng Zhongming was in very truth lodged at the Continental Hotel; if the Wang household kept an extra room for him to stay in, for convenience of business, or because he was sometimes late returning, that too would be in reason, for his relation with Wang was too close. As to whether Zeng Zhongming's wife, Miss Fang Junbi, lodged there with him, we do not know; that she too took three bullets and fell into a pool of blood—Comrade Wang Luqiao made no such report, and had there been one, he would by no means have hidden it, nor needed to shun the telling.
Whether Wang's attendants were really bare-handed, "without so much as a single gun," I cannot affirm, and it should be set down as an open question.

I heard only two bursts of gunfire, some five or six reports, unlike the several separate volleys spoken of in the text. As to whether five or six persons were wounded, at the time it was not convenient to verify, and afterward I saw no such report in the newspapers either.

Beyond this, there is much more that might be picked at; but I think it best not to be too long-winded, and the most important thing is first to say a word on why the error came about—the shooting of the wrong man.
To pass it off in the four words "careless and inattentive" would show too light and slighting a touch, and would wrong the reconnaissance pains we had spent beforehand.
To say that Wang Jingwei and Zeng Zhongming, the two of them, had that night changed rooms for the moment would seem a little too pat a way of rounding it off, and might not carry conviction.

In fact, one cannot but own that it was because our reconnaissance work was not thorough enough. Beforehand we knew only that No. 27 Gao Lang Street was Wang's residence, and did not know that there was also that building, No. 25, which had been knocked through into it.

Had it not been that, on instinct, we mistook the man lying prone under the bed for Wang, we should surely have gone on searching, until we found Wang. Even had we not known beforehand that the two houses were made one, we should have discovered it in the course of the search.

Had Zeng Zhongming not crept under the bed and hidden his head, both Luqiao and Jiansheng knew him, and without the sanction of a command to kill, would on no account have fired on him. That is to say, could they but have seen Zeng Zhongming's face clearly through the hole in the door, all that followed would have been quite different.
By reason of these three factors—some of them men's ill contriving, some the coincidence of chance—there came about, through crossed purposes and mischance, this great and grievous reverse.

By the way the thing was carried out that night—in the deep of night, through the hewing of the lock with a sharp axe, the kicking-in of the door with a great foot, the firing shot on shot at those of the Wang house who came out at the noise, and then the hacking of a great hole in the room-door—this whole string of actions not only dragged the time out very long, but gave off a noise to startle the neighbors on every side; and though within and without there were men on watch, one had to guard against a telephoned alarm, or the sudden arrival of the local detectives at any moment. Whether, then, there was some flurry in the mind, is very hard to say.

I have thought too: had we not, at the time, been carried away by feeling, but been a little cooler, held our breath, waited and done it another night, and been a little more unhurried on the spot—perhaps we might have brought it off at a single stroke, and this passage of history would then have been rewritten.

For this strange and tangled piece of action-work, Luqiao and I, between ourselves, went over it in reckoning more than once; the causes of the error, besides the untruth of the reconnaissance, must be laid to a kind of illusion of the mind. Luqiao, ever the hearty man, held that there might well have been "rashness" and "recklessness" in it, but that to say there was on the spot such "flurry" as to fire wildly at random would be far too much. In sum, we both came to feel: since the thing had not succeeded, more words were of no use, and we ought to bear the responsibility for this failure.

Truly, we still meant to marshal our forces afresh and make another attempt; but though we had a spare valor yet to spend, the time was already against us. On the very second night there came a telegram, urgently summoning the writer to return first, by himself, to Chongqing; and the day after I bought passage and set off.
Zeng Zhongming's grave wounding and death—the former was a case of being hit by mistake, the latter came of losing too much blood and of doctoring too poor. This was a thing to regret.

For the death of Zeng Zhongming, Wang Jingwei wrote a piece, "An Account of the Conduct of Mr. Zeng Zhongming," to show his mourning; and though it was rich alike in feeling and in style, there was withal something of a pose in it.

Besides this, Wang wrote of his own hand a long piece, "To Cite One Instance," in defense of his "advocacy of peace," and brought forward the record of the "Fifty-fourth Standing Committee Meeting of the Supreme National Defense Council" to overawe men with. In truth, where was his "advocacy of peace"? It was plainly a "suing for surrender"—only that the name sounds better.

After Wang, on the ninth of April, publicly issued "To Cite One Instance," the Generalissimo, Mr. Chiang, on the eleventh of April, set down his feeling in his own hand: "Many a false and treacherous man have I seen, but never one so base as Wang." At the same time the Central Supervisory Committee member of the Chinese Nationalist Party, the venerable Wu Jingheng (Zhihui), issued, aimed at that piece, an essay, "A Further Reading of Wang Jingwei's 'To Cite One Instance.'" Not only did it upbraid Wang's fickleness to the very dregs, but in describing his falseness and baseness it cut, as it were, into the very wood three-tenths of an inch deep. Reading the whole essay through, we came to know: that Wang had, in that record of the National Defense meeting, changed the beams and swapped the pillars, and worked his hand upon it. With a character like this, was he anything like a statesman?

The work of sanctioning Wang Jingwei did not stop at this; afterward, as the circumstances shifted and changed, there were developments on many sides besides, and our comrades at the work had, too, yet more sacrifices to make!
